verses.zh: 我的心灵消耗，我的日子灭尽；坟墓为我预备好了。
verses.en: My spirit is broken,[NOTE:1] my days have faded out;[NOTE:2] the grave[NOTE:3] awaits me.
notes: The verb חָבַל (khaval, “to act badly”) in the Piel means “to ruin.” The Pual translation with “my spirit” as the subject means “broken” in the sense of finished (not in the sense of humbled as in Ps 51).
The verb זָעַךְ (zaʿaq, equivalent of Aramaic דָעַק [daʿaq]) means “to be extinguished.” It only occurs here in the Hebrew.

The plural “graves” could be simply an intensification, a plural of extension (see GKC 397 §124.c), or a reference to the graveyard. Coverdale had: “I am harde at deathes dore.” The Hebrew expression simply reads “graves for me.” It probably means that graves await him.

verses.zh: 真有戏笑我的在我这里，我眼常见他们惹动我。
verses.en: Surely mockery[NOTE:1] is with me;[NOTE:2] my eyes must dwell on their hostility.[NOTE:3]
notes: The noun is the abstract noun, “mockery.” It indicates that he is the object of derision. But many commentators either change the word to “mockers” (Tur-Sinai, NEB), or argue that the form in the text is a form of the participle (Gordis).
E. Dhorme (Job, 243) interprets the preposition to mean “aimed at me.”

The meaning of הַמְּרוֹתָם (hammerotam) is unclear, and the versions offer no help. If the MT is correct, it would probably be connected to מָרָה (marah, “to be rebellious”) and the derived form something like “hostility; provocation.” But some commentators suggest it should be related to מָרֹרוֹת (marorot, “bitter things”). Others have changed both the noun and the verb to obtain something like “My eye is weary of their contentiousness” (Holscher), or “mine eyes are wearied by your stream of peevish complaints” (G. R. Driver, “Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 78). There is no alternative suggestion that is compelling.

verses.zh: 愿主拿凭据给我，自己为我作保。在你以外谁肯与我击掌呢？
verses.en: Set my pledge[NOTE:1] beside you.Who else will put up security for me?[NOTE:2]
notes: Job shows his desperation in lacking anyone to act as a guarantor on his behalf by asking God to accept himself as his own guarantor, a somewhat self-contradictory notion.tc The MT has two imperatives: “Set (down), pledge me, with you.” Most commentators think that the second imperative, עָרְבֵנִי (ʿareveni, “pledge security for), should be repointed as a noun, עֵרְבֹנִי (ʿerevoni, “my pledge of security”) and take it to say, “Set my pledge beside you.” A. B. Davidson (Job, 126) suggests that the first verb means “give a pledge,” and so the two similar verbs would be emphatic: “Give a pledge, be my surety.” However, the verb שִׂים (sim, “set”) does not work with other verbs in this manner in any other contexts.
The idiom is “to strike the hand.” Here the wording is a little different, “Who is he that will strike himself into my hand?”

verses.zh: 因你使他们心不明理，所以你必不高举他们。
verses.en: Because[NOTE:1] you have closed their[NOTE:2] minds to understanding,therefore you will not exalt them.[NOTE:3]
notes: This half-verse gives the reason for the next half-verse.
The pronoun their refers to Job’s friends. They have not pledged security for him because God has hidden or sealed off their understanding.

The object “them” is supplied. This is the simplest reading of the line, taking the verb as an active Polel. Some suggest that the subject is “their hand” and the verb is to be translated “is not raised.” This would carry through the thought of the last verse, but it is not necessary to the point.

verses.zh: 控告他的朋友、以朋友为可抢夺的，连他儿女的眼睛也要失明。
verses.en: If a man denounces his friends for personal gain,[NOTE:1] the eyes of his children will fail.
notes: Heb “for a portion.” This verse is rather obscure. The words are not that difficult, but the sense of them in this context is. Some take the idea to mean “he denounces his friends for a portion,” and others have a totally different idea of “he invites his friends to share with him.” The former fits the context better, indicating that Job’s friends speak out against him for some personal gain. The second half of the verse then promises that his children will suffer loss for this attempt at gain. The line is surely proverbial. A number of other interpretations can be found in the commentaries.

verses.zh: 神使我作了民中的笑谈；他们也吐唾沫在我脸上。
verses.en: He has made me[NOTE:1] a byword[NOTE:2] to people;I am the one in whose face they spit.[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb is the third person, and so God is likely the subject. The LXX has “you have made me.” So most commentators clarify the verb in some such way. However, without an expressed subject it can also be taken as a passive.
The word “byword” is related to the word translated “proverb” in the Bible (מָשָׁל, mashal). Job’s case is so well known that he is synonymous with afflictions and with abuse by people.

The word תֹפֶת (tofet) is a hapax legomenon. The expression is “and a spitting in/to the face I have become,” i.e., “I have become one in whose face people spit.” Various suggestions have been made, including a link to Tophet, but they are weak. The verse as it exists in the MT is fine, and fits the context well.

verses.zh: 我的眼睛因忧愁昏花；我的百体好像影儿。
verses.en: My eyes have grown dim[NOTE:1] with grief;my whole frame[NOTE:2] is but a shadow.
notes: See the usage of this verb in Gen 27:1 and Deut 34:7. Usually it is age that causes the failing eyesight, but here it is the grief.

The word יְצֻרִים (yetsurim), here with a suffix, occurs only here in the Bible. The word is related to יָצַר (yatsar, “to form, fashion”). And so Targum Job has “my forms,” and the Vulgate “my members.” The Syriac uses “thoughts” to reflect יֵצֶר (yetser). Some have followed this to interpret, “all my thoughts have dissolved into shadows.” But the parallel with “eye” would suggest “form.” The plural “my forms, all of them” would refer to the whole body.

verses.zh: 正直人因此必惊奇；无辜的人要兴起攻击不敬虔之辈。
verses.en: Upright men are appalled[NOTE:1] at this;the innocent man is troubled[NOTE:2] with the godless.
notes: This verb שָׁמַם (shamam, “appalled”) is the one found in Isa 52:14, translated there “astonished.”
The verb means “to rouse oneself to excitement.” It naturally means “to be agitated; to be stirred up.”

verses.zh: 然而，义人要持守所行的道；手洁的人要力上加力。
verses.en: But the righteous man holds to his way,and the one with clean hands grows stronger.[NOTE:1]
notes: The last two words are the imperfect verb יֹסִיף (yosif) which means “he adds,” and the abstract noun “energy, strength.” This noun is not found elsewhere; its Piel verb occurs in Job 4:4 and 16:5. “he increases strength.”

verses.zh: 至于你们众人，可以再来辩论吧！你们中间，我找不着一个智慧人。
verses.en: “But turn, all of you,[NOTE:1] and come[NOTE:2] now![NOTE:3] I will not find a wise man among you.
notes: The form says “all of them.” Several editors would change it to “all of you,” but the lack of concord is not surprising; the vocative elsewhere uses the third person (see Mic 1:2; see also GKC 441 §135.r).
The first verb, the jussive, means “to return”; the second verb, the imperative, means “to come.” The two could be taken as a hendiadys, the first verb becoming adverbial: “to come again.”
Instead of the exact correspondence between coordinate verbs, other combinations occur—here we have a jussive and an imperative (see GKC 386 §120.e).

verses.zh: 我的日子已经过了；我的谋算、我心所想望的已经断绝。
verses.en: My days have passed; my plans[NOTE:1] are shattered,even[NOTE:2] the desires[NOTE:3] of my heart.
notes: This term usually means “plans; devices” in a bad sense, although it can be used of God’s plans (see e.g., Zech 8:15).
Although not in the Hebrew text, “even” is supplied in the translation because this line is in apposition to the preceding.

This word has been linked to the root יָרַשׁ (yarash, “to inherit”) yielding a meaning “the possessions of my heart.” But it is actually to be connected to אָרַשׁ (ʾarash, “to desire”) cognate to the Akkadian eresu, “desire.” The LXX has “limbs,” which may come from an Aramaic word for “ropes.” An emendation based on the LXX would be risky.

verses.zh: 他们以黑夜为白昼，说：亮光近乎黑暗。
verses.en: These men[NOTE:1] change[NOTE:2] night into day;they say,[NOTE:3] ‘The light is near in the face of darkness.’[NOTE:4]
notes: The verse simply has the plural, “they change.” But since this verse seems to be a description of his friends, a clarification of the referent in the translation is helpful.
The same verb שִׂים (sim, “set”) is used this way in Isa 5:20: “…who change darkness into light.”
The rest of the verse makes better sense if it is interpreted as what his friends say.

This expression is open to alternative translations: (1) It could mean that they say in the face of darkness, “Light is near.” (2) It could also mean “The light is near the darkness” or “The light is nearer than the darkness.”

verses.zh: 我若盼望阴间为我的房屋，若下榻在黑暗中，
verses.en: If[NOTE:1] I hope for the grave to be my home,if I spread out my bed in darkness,
notes: The clause begins with אִם (ʾim) which here has more of the sense of “since.” E. Dhorme (Job, 253) takes a rather rare use of the word to get “Can I hope again” (see also GKC 475 §150.f for the caveat).

verses.zh: 若对朽坏说：你是我的父；对虫说：你是我的母亲姊妹；
verses.en: if I cry out[NOTE:1] to corruption,[NOTE:2] ‘You are my father,’and to the worm, ‘My mother,’ or ‘My sister,’
notes: This is understood because the conditional clauses seem to run to the apodosis in v. 15.

The word שַׁחַת (shakhat) may be the word “corruption” from a root שָׁחַת (shakhat, “to destroy”) or a word “pit” from שׁוּחַ (shuakh, “to sink down”). The same problem surfaces in Ps 16:10, where it is parallel to “Sheol.” E. F. Sutcliffe, The Old Testament and the Future Life, 76ff., defends the meaning “corruption.” But many commentators here take it to mean “the grave” in harmony with “Sheol.” But in this verse “worms” would suggest “corruption” is better.

verses.zh: 这样，我的指望在哪里呢？我所指望的谁能看见呢？
verses.en: where then[NOTE:1] is my hope?And my hope,[NOTE:2] who sees it?
notes: The adverb אֵפוֹ (ʾefo, “then”) plays an enclitic role here (see Job 4:7).

The repetition of “my hope” in the verse has thrown the versions off, and their translations have led commentators also to change the second one to something like “goodness,” on the assumption that a word cannot be repeated in the same verse. The word actually carries two different senses here. The first would be the basic meaning “hope,” but the second a metonymy of cause, namely, what hope produces, what will be seen.

verses.zh: 等到安息在尘土中，这指望必下到阴间的门闩那里了。
verses.en: Will[NOTE:1] it[NOTE:2] go down to the barred gates[NOTE:3] of death?Will[NOTE:4] we descend[NOTE:5] together into the dust?”
notes: It is natural to assume that this verse continues the interrogative clause of the preceding verse.
The plural form of the verb probably refers to the two words, or the two senses of the word in the preceding verse. Hope and what it produces will perish with Job.
The Hebrew word בַּדִּים (baddim) describes the “bars” or “bolts” of Sheol, referring (by synecdoche) to the “gates of Sheol.” The LXX has “with me to Sheol,” and many adopt that as “by my side.”
The conjunction אִם (ʾim) confirms the interrogative interpretation.

The translation follows the LXX and the Syriac versions with the change of vocalization in the MT. The MT has the noun “rest,” yielding, “will our rest be together in the dust?” The verb נָחַת (nakhat) in Aramaic means “to go down; to descend.” If that is the preferred reading—and it almost is universally accepted here—then it would be spelled נֵחַת (nekhat). In either case the point of the verse is clearly describing death and going to the grave.

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Job expresses his feelings about his current condition (Job 17:1-2,6-7,11).

- He describes his three comforters in Job 17:2a,4,5,10,12.

- Job still calls out to God even though he questions His care (Job 17:3-4,15-16). The
main questions are

- God, will You be my pledge and guarantor?

- Where is my hope? (Job 17:15, cf. 7:6)

- Remember, Job 16 and 17 form a literary unit.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

The grave is ready for me.

17:1-2 Job expresses his feelings in several poetic lines in Job 17:1-11.

- my spirit is broken, Job 17:1a

- my days are extinguished, Job. 17:1a

- the grave is ready for me, Job 17:1b

- mockers are with me, Job 17:2a

- he is a byword of the people, Job 17:6a

- all his members are as a shadow, Job 17:7b

- his days are past, Job 17:11a

- his plans are torn, Job 17:11a

- the wishes of his heart are torn, Job 17:11b

17:1 "spirit" This is ruah (BDB 924).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

▣ "broken" There are many meanings connected to this root. The
VERB (BDB 287 II, KB 285, Pual PERFECT) normally means,
"act corruptly," but in the Pual it can mean "broken"
(cf. Isa. 10:27).

The MT has זעך (BDB 276, KB 276, Niphal
PERFECT). This is the only use
of the Niphal stem of this root in the OT. Most usages of the
root are in Qal.

Some emend it to דעך (BDB 200), which also means
"go out" or "be extinguished" (NASB, cf. Job 18:5,6).

The NJB makes two emendations to this line of poetry, but UBS Text
Project, p. 40, supports the MT (B rating, meaning some doubt).

▣ "the grave" The
MT has the PLURAL, which
is where NJB gets "grave diggers." Job is expecting to die
(cf. Job 17:13-16).

17:2 "mockers" This refers to Job's comforters.

▣ "their provocation"
The VERBAL is a Hiphil
INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (BDB
598, KB 632). Job accuses his comforters of being "disobedient to
God," "rebellious toward God."

▣ "dwells" This VERB (BDB 533, KB 529, Qal
JUSSIVE) means "to
lodge with," "pass the night with." The other English
translations, excluding the NKJV and NRSV, translate it idiomatically.
The comments and accusations of Job's comforters (cf. Job 16:2a) are
ever before him. They haunt his mind and heart, but he thinks their
words are an attack on God, as well as himself!

3"Lay
down, now, a pledge for me with Yourself;
Who is there that will be my
guarantor?
4For
You have kept their heart from understanding,
Therefore You will not exalt them.
5He who informs against
friends for a share of the spoil,
The eyes of his children also will
languish.

17:3-4 Job addresses God in prayer (i.e., two Qal IMPERATIVES). He is

- asking God to be his assurance (pledge, guarantor)

- he is still seeking the aid of a heavenly advocate (cf. Job 16:19; 19:25-27)

- AB (p. 120) suggests a revocalization that turns this into Job's offer to make a pledge
to God hoping He will offer His pledge back

17:3b

NASB
"be my guarantor"

NKJV
"will shake hands with me"

NRSV
"will give surety for me"

NJB
"cares to slap his hand on mine"

JPSOA
"will give his hand on my behalf"

REB
"will pledge himself for me"

NET
"will put up security for me?"

The MT has "who will strike himself into my hand" (BDB 1075,
KB 1785, Niphal IMPERFECT).
This physical gesture denoted the ratification of a pledge (cf. Prov.
6:1; 17:18; in a negative sense in Prov. 11:15; 22:26).

17:4 The sovereignty of God, which has often been affirmed by the three friends, is
used to assure the divine judgment of the friends.

- God has "hidden" (BDB 860, KB 1049, Qal PERFECT) their
hearts/minds from understanding (cf. Job 12:20)

- God will not exalt them (nor their children, Job 17:5b) because they attacked a friend
for personal gain, Job 17:5 (cf. Job 13:7-11)

The last line of Job 17:4 can be a prayer for God to

- not let the three friends be exalted (cf. Exod. 15:1; Ps. 37:34; Prov. 4:8)

- not let the three friends triumph (BDB 926, KB 1202, Polel IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 41:11)

- this VERB stem is used of raising children (cf. Isa. 1:2; 23:4) and children are mentioned
in Job 17:5b. If so, this would be an idiom for their descendants to be cut off (i.e., no posterity).

17:5 "for a share" This NOUN (BDB 324 I) means "portion."
It can refer

- positively – Job 31:2

- negatively – Job 27:13

Here it refers to the three friends attacking Job to promote their sense
of acceptance with God (cf. Job 13:8,10).

The NASB Study Bible (p. 709) and The Jerome Bible Commentary (p.
521) both think it is a proverb that Job quoted "to counter the
false accusations of his friends."

17:6 The sovereign God not only acted toward the three friends but also toward Job. There is
some doubt who this verse refers to.

- the SINGULAR of Job 17:5a

- God

▣ "a byword" The NOUN (BDB 605) usually means
"a proverb" or "a parable," but here it is parallel with "one at
whom men spit," so it must have a negative connotation (cf. Num. 12:14; Deut. 25:9;
Job 30:10; Isa. 50:6). Apparently Job was being used as an example of how "the two
ways" worked! This was very painful for a righteous man (cf. Job. 17:8-9).

17:7b This is an ambiguous line of poetry. It could relate to Job 16:8, where Job
describes his body as "shriveled up."

However, the word "shadow" (BDB 853) can have the connotation
of death. This imagery is surely referred to in Job 17:12-16.

- the presence of darkness (BDB 365)

- Sheol (BDB 982, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL, I. B.)

- in the darkness (BDB 365, cf. Job 3:4,5; 10:21; 15:22,23)

- the pit (BDB 1001)

- to the worm (cf. Job 7:5; 21:26)

- go down with me to Sheol

- go down into the dust (BDB 779)

Job is contemplating the imminence of his own death.

"members"

NJB, REB
"limbs"

"all shapes"

NET

The MT has יצרים (BDB 428), which is found
only here in the OT. BDB gives two options.

- "members" or "limbs"

- "forms" or "shapes"

17:8-9 These verses use several phrases/words to describe faithful followers,
of which Job considers himself to be, but the three friends now do not.

- the upright (BDB 449)

- the innocent (BDB 667)

- the righteous (BDB 843)

- he who has clean hands (BDB 373 CONSTRUCT BDB 388)

It is possible to view Job 17:8-9 as a sarcastic reference as to how the
three comforters view themselves.

It is also possible that it is a general statement that righteous people
would be appalled at the unfounded accusations and innuendoes of the
three friends against Job.

17:10 Job encourages his attackers to try again (lit. "come on again," BDB 97,
KB 112, Qal IMPERFECT and Qal IMPERATIVE), but
he is sure there is no wise man (BDB 314) among them!

Job characterizes their words in Job 17:12. They promise Job good
things/times if he would acknowledge his sin and repent, but they only
taunt a good, innocent, blameless man!

17:11 "plans" The NOUN (BDB 273) is usually used
of the plans of evil people. Only here does it denote a godly plan. It is paralleled to
"the wishes of my heart."

17:12 The "they" refers to the three comforters. Their accusations
have exacerbated Job's pain, doubt, and confusion.

17:13 "Sheol" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL, I. B.

17:16

NASB
"will it go down with me to Sheol"

NKJV, LXX
"will they go down to the gates of Sheol"

NRSV, Peshitta
"will it go down to the bars of Sheol"

JPSOA
"will it descend to Sheol"

REB
"I cannot atake them with me down to Sheol"

The MT has "the bars of Sheol will they do down together?"
There are several questions.

- The UBS Text Project (p. 43) suggests that the first phrase, "the bars of Sheol"
should be translated "with me (into) Sheol" ("C" rating), which is a revocalization.
This change is supported by the Aramaic Targums.

- The other question is to what or whom does "it" refer?

- in the MT it is PLURAL and may refer to the three comforters of Job 17:12

- the imagery of "father" and "mother" of Job 17:14

- the "hope" of Job 17:15

- The last word of the last line of poetry in Job 17:16 in the MT is "rest"
(BDB 629, cf. Eccl. 6:5), but a revocalization makes it "descend," which
fits the parallelism better. The UBS Text Project (p. 44) gives "descend"
a C rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "into the dust"
This (BDB 779) is an idiom for death (cf. Job 7:21; 20:11; 21:26; Ps.
22:15,29; 30:9; Isa. 26:19; Dan. 12:2).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide
commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have.
You, the Bible and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You
must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the
major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought
provoking, not definitive.

- Explain Job 17:3 in your own words.

- To whom does Job 17:4 refer?

- How does Job 17:5 apply to Job's three comforters?

- How does Job 17:8-9 fit into the literary flow of the chapter?

- Who is the "they" of Job 17:12?

- To what does "hope" in Job 17:15 refer?

- What/who does "it" of Job 17:16 refer?
